Foreword
Identity used to be a predictable, bounded problem.
For years, identity management meant keeping the basics ticking along: provisioning users,
managing standard groups, and handling the core Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) lifecycle. You
built your directory, mapped out your standard access patterns, and tried not to change things
unless you absolutely had to.
Then, the cloud completely shattered those boundaries.
First came the operational complexity of rapid mergers and acquisitions, forcing identity teams
to stitch completely different environments together, inherit mounds of tenant technical debt,
and manage complex external collaborations overnight. Right alongside this corporate sprawl
came a wave of sophisticated cloud threats. Attackers realized they didn't need to exploit
firewall vulnerabilities when they could just steal a session token, abuse a misconfigured app
registration, or target a stale guest account.
To fight back, our identity infrastructure had to evolve fast. What used to be a simple sign-on
process ballooned into a massive ecosystem of multi-tenant architectures, strict governance
workflows, and complex webs of Conditional Access policies.
And just as we started getting a handle on that, the landscape shifted again.
We entered the era of AI and autonomous systems. Today, identity isn't just about human
users or traditional software workloads. The moment an AI agent can call an API, read
corporate data, or take actions in a business system, it becomes a brand-new identity surface.
Managing and governing these Agent IDs, tracking who owns them, what they can access, and
preventing " agent sprawl ", is the newest, highest-stakes frontier for modern identity teams.
This is why identity is now the ultimate control plane for almost everything we do in the cloud.
It decides who or what gets access, from what device, to which applications, and under what
level of risk.
Keeping all of this in your head is a massive challenge for any admin, architect, or security
engineer. That's exactly why we need this book, and why I'm so glad Pramiti wrote it.
Having worked alongside Pramiti at Microsoft, I've seen firsthand her ability to bridge the gap
between deep product engineering and messy, real-world customer deployments. She
understands the technology inside out, but more importantly, she understands the daily
operational grind: the hybrid technical debt, legacy dependencies, stressful audits, endless
admin portals, and the constant barrage of alerts.
This book reflects that practical mindset. It doesn't treat Microsoft Entra ID as a disconnected
collection of features; it treats identity as a cohesive system. Pramiti takes you from the
foundational building blocks, such as tenants, users, groups, and Conditional Access, right

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: ISBN 978-1-80611-601-0
chunks.content:
through to the advanced capabilities modern environments demand: Identity Governance,
Lifecycle Workflows, Privileged Identity Management (PIM), Workload Identities, Global
Secure Access, and now, the critical task of securing AI agent infrastructure.
This end-to-end view is critical because you can't solve identity security with a single feature.
You don't " do Zero Trust " by flipping a single toggle. You don't protect highly privileged roles by
just asking people to be careful. You can't manage joiners, movers, and leavers on a
spreadsheet forever. And you certainly can't leave your identity architecture as an
afterthought. You need a model. You need patterns. You need to know how the pieces fit
together.
That's where this book shines. It is built for the people doing the actual work. Whether you are
designing a brand-new architecture, cleaning up a stale tenant, navigating a high-stakes M&A
integration, or modernizing away from legacy on-premises Active Directory, this book gives
you actionable guidance.
The threat landscape has evolved, and attackers have figured out that identity is the easiest
way into an organization. They aren't breaking in; they are logging in. Token theft, consent
phishing, over-privileged apps, and stale guest accounts are no longer edge cases, they are
everyday realities.
Microsoft Entra ID gives us an incredibly powerful toolkit to defend against these threats, but
knowing how to architect and deploy it effectively is the real challenge.
Whether you are a seasoned identity architect, a security engineer, or an admin who just
inherited a messy tenant and is wondering where to start, this book will build your confidence.
It will take you from simply knowing a feature exists to knowing how to design and operate it
responsibly.
Identity is far too critical to be treated as a pile of random settings. It requires architecture,
governance, automation, and continuous learning. Pramiti has distilled years of hands-on
experience into a clear, actionable blueprint to help you get it right.
Keep this book on your desk. You're going to need it.
Merill Fernando
Principal Product Manager at Microsoft
Contributors
About the author
Pramiti Bhatnagar is a seasoned technology leader with more than 20 years of deep expertise
across Microsoft's security and identity ecosystem, including Microsoft Entra, Microsoft
Purview, Microsoft Defender, and Microsoft Security Copilot. She holds an honours degree in
Applied Psychology from the University of Delhi and a range of industry-recognized
certifications, including CIPM, CISSP, and Microsoft Certified: Cybersecurity Architect Expert.
Pramiti currently serves as a Principal Product Manager for Microsoft Entra, where she focuses
on the Entra Suite with a particular emphasis on Microsoft Security Copilot and Security for AI.

She is a respected public speaker, regularly presenting at industry forums such as the
Australian Information Security Association (AISA) and ISACA. Beyond her product
leadership, Pramiti is committed to developing the next generation of security professionals.
She actively mentors emerging talent through the Global Mentorship Initiative (GMI) and
the Australian Women in Security Network (AWSN). She was a finalist for Cybersecurity
Leader of the Year at the Women in Digital Awards.
About the reviewer
Abbas Kudrati is the Regional Chief Identity Security and AI Advisor at Silverfort and the
former Chief Cybersecurity Advisor at Microsoft Asia. A neurodiverse cybersecurity leader and
a dedicated advocate for the ADHD community, Abbas brings a unique cognitive perspective to
his deep expertise in AI Security, Identity Security, Zero Trust Architecture, Governance, Risk,
and Compliance (GRC), and Cloud Security. He provides strategic and technical guidance to a
number of startups, including SquareX, Aona.ai, and PriviEzi, as well as leading institutions
such as EC-Council and Vinnies Victoria, while actively mentoring the cybersecurity
community.
A bestselling author and renowned keynote speaker, Abbas has authored industry-recognized
books such as Threat Hunting in the Cloud, Zero Trust Journey Across the Digital Estate, Cloud
Container Security and Managing Risks in Digital Transformation. He also serves as a Professor
of Practice at La Trobe University and is a Fellow of the Australian Information Security
Association (AISA).

Preface
Identity used to be simple. Users signed in, opened applications, and anything inside the
network was assumed to be trustworthy. That model worked when systems were centralized
and the pace of change was slow. Today, the landscape is very different. Workloads run across
clouds, users work from anywhere, and access extends far beyond employees. Partners,
customers, applications, and automated workloads all require controlled access, often at
massive scale. The perimeter has dissolved, and identity has become the primary control plane.
With that shift, every access decision matters more. It is no longer enough to confirm who is
requesting access; you must also understand context, risk, and intent. Zero Trust emerges here
not as a slogan, but as a practical necessity. At the same time, operational demands have
grown. Managing identity lifecycles, governing access, controlling privileged roles, and
responding to identity-driven threats all require a level of rigor that many organizations are
still developing.
Microsoft Entra is built for this new reality, but realizing its value takes more than enabling
features. It requires a mindset, a way of thinking about identity architecturally, as a strategic
layer rather than a background service. This book is written with that perspective. It walks
through the core building blocks, the decisions that shape real-world deployments, and the
patterns that consistently hold up under pressure.
By the end, you should see identity not just as something to administer, but as something you
can intentionally design to strengthen security, reduce friction, and support how your
organization truly operates.
Who this book is for
This book is for identity administrators, system administrators, security engineers, cloud
architects, and IT professionals responsible for securing and governing enterprise access. If you
manage hybrid environments, enforce Zero Trust, automate lifecycle processes, or protect
against identity-based threats, this guide is for you. A foundational understanding of
networking, IAM, and cloud concepts will help you get the most from this book.
What this book covers

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 1, Introduction to Microsoft Entra, establishes the foundational concepts of identity by
chunks.content:
Chapter 1, Introduction to Microsoft Entra, establishes the foundational concepts of identity by
introducing the Identity, Authentication, Authorization, Accountability (IAAA) model and
explaining how these principles shape modern access control. It covers the basics of identity
and access management and positions the Microsoft identity platform as the core engine
behind authentication and authorization across Microsoft services. The chapter concludes
with an overview of the Microsoft Entra product family, providing a clear map of the
capabilities that will be explored in depth throughout the book.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 2, Fundamentals of Microsoft Entra ID, introduces the essential building blocks of
chunks.content:
Chapter 2, Fundamentals of Microsoft Entra ID, introduces the essential building blocks of
modern access management, such as Single Sign-On (SSO) and Multi-Factor Authentication
(MFA). It explains how Microsoft Entra RBAC provides structured, least-privilege access
control and explores the authentication methods that underpin secure sign-ins. The chapter
also covers Conditional Access and protected actions, showing how policy-driven enforcement
strengthens security while adapting to user context and risk.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 3, Implementing Microsoft Entra ID, guides you through selecting and implementing the
chunks.content:
Chapter 3, Implementing Microsoft Entra ID, guides you through selecting and implementing the
right identity model for your organization. It covers core operational tasks such as user and
group management, the use of Administrative Units for delegated administration, and the
essential security settings every Entra tenant should configure. The chapter concludes with an
overview of end-user self-service capabilities, highlighting how thoughtful design can reduce
operational overhead while improving user experience.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 4, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, explains how Microsoft Entra provides managed
chunks.content:
Chapter 4, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, explains how Microsoft Entra provides managed
domain capabilities for applications that rely on traditional directory protocols. It outlines
when and why to use Domain Services, how it integrates into your environment, without
needing to maintain on-premises domain controllers.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 5, AI in Microsoft Entra, introduces AI capabilities in Microsoft Entra. It discusses
chunks.content:
Chapter 5, AI in Microsoft Entra, introduces AI capabilities in Microsoft Entra. It discusses
Security Copilot and explores how AI-driven reasoning enhances identity security, incident
response, and operational efficiency. It also explains Microsoft Entra Agent ID, the identity
foundation for autonomous and semi-autonomous agents accessing resources across cloud
services.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 6, Microsoft Entra Entitlement Management, explores Entitlement Management as the
chunks.content:
Chapter 6, Microsoft Entra Entitlement Management, explores Entitlement Management as the
foundation for governing access at scale through access packages, catalogs, and access reviews.
It explains how to streamline user access and enforce approval and review processes. The focus

Microsoft Entra is Microsoft's cloud-native Identity and Access Management (IAM)
solution. It is a comprehensive suite designed idx_97ee6a09 to unify identity and access idx_26589447 management across
digital ecosystems. It ensures seamless and secure interactions between people, devices,
applications, and services, empowering organizations to streamline their operations while
safeguarding sensitive data. Rooted in the principles of zero-trust, Microsoft Entra integrates
cutting-edge tools and technologies to address the evolving challenges of digital security. Its
offerings include identity governance, access control, and secure network access, all aimed at
fortifying organizational resilience against cyber threats.
Microsoft Entra embraces dynamic identity solutions for both human and non-human entities.
Through its innovative frameworks, it supports hybrid environments, enabling organizations
to transition smoothly between on-premises infrastructure and cloud-based systems. With its

Identity fundamentals
A digital identity idx_4f265957 is a foundational concept in the realm of digital security and system
architecture. Each entity that interacts idx_3d869cfc with a computer system has an identity. This includes
not only human but also non-human identities like devices and applications. A digital identity
comprises a collection of unique identifiers or attributes that distinguish an individual,
software component, or machine. Examples idx_bbbcfb3c of such identifiers include email addresses,
usernames, MAC addresses, and IP addresses. Digital identities serve a critical role in
authenticating users and authorizing access to various resources. The fundamentals of
computer identity focus on the principles of identification, authentication, authorization, and
accountability, all of which are necessary for enabling secure and seamless interactions in
virtual environments.
Identification
Identification is the initial step in establishing an identity. It involves recognizing and
distinguishing entities within a digital ecosystem. This is usually done using identifiers like
usernames, email addresses, or idx_8f60a6c4 unique device IDs that serve as the primary markers to
differentiate one entity from another. These identifiers are critical for tracking and managing

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 5, AI in Microsoft Entra
chunks.content:
digital identities, ensuring that each entity is uniquely identifiable within the system.
Identification refers to the process by which a subject asserts an identity. To initiate
authentication, authorization, and auditing procedures, the subject must present their identity
to the system. This may involve entering a username, swiping a smartcard, or presenting
biometric data such as facial features, a hand, or a fingerprint to a scanning device. A core
principle is that all subjects must have a unique identity.
Authentication
Authentication is the process of confirming that an entity presenting an identity is genuinely
who or what it claims to be by checking idx_df1a305e one or more credentials against a database of
authorized identities, such as user accounts. The credentials used for authentication are
confidential and must be properly secured at all times. This involves the use of credentials,
such as passwords, biometric data, security tokens, or digital certificates. Authentication is
sometimes shortened as AuthN. Single-factor authentication relies on one method of
idx_c6d4edbd verification, while multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds layers of security by requiring
with your book section in the Preface to unlock them instantly and maximize your
learning.

Chapter 1 4
two or more proofs of identity. MFA is a security measure that requires users to provide more
than one piece of evidence to prove their identities. These are:
Something you know, like a password
Something you have, like a security token
Something you are, like a biometric
MFA must be a combination of two or more of the above. For example, a PIN and password
cannot be called MFA because both fall under something you know. A PIN and a biometric is
MFA because they are a combination of something you know and something you are.
Single Sign-On (SSO) allows users idx_3260e047 to authenticate once and later seamlessly authenticate to
resources that rely on the same identity.
Identification and authentication normally occur as a single two-step process.
Authorization
Just because an entity is authenticated, it does not mean that it has the authorization to access
resources. Authorization is the idx_9aaa0660 process of determining what actions or permissions the entity
has within the system. It ensures that only entities with the appropriate roles, attributes, or
permissions can access specific resources or perform certain functions. For example,
administrators can grant access to files based on user's role. Authorization is sometimes
shortened as AuthZ.
Accountability
Accountability is the process of holding users accountable for the actions they take.
Accountability ties the identity to idx_ba857b90 actions and behaviors within a digital system. By
maintaining logs and tracking activity, organizations can monitor how identities interact with
resources, detect anomalies, and enforce security policies. For instance, auditing can document
instances when a user accesses, modifies, or deletes a file. This helps ensure accountability
within the system. Accountability not only aids in addressing security incidents but also
supports regulatory compliance and auditing efforts.
Together, authentication, authorization, and idx_ab8b6883 accountability provide for nonrepudiation.
Nonrepudiation ensures that a user who performed an action cannot deny performing it or
that it occurred.
Identity provider (IdP)
An identity provider is a system that creates, manages, and maintains identity information and
offers authentication, authorization, and idx_1bd7fdc4 auditing services. With modern idx_99361a2c authentication all
services are provided by a centralized identity provider. By utilizing a central identity provider,
•

organizations are able to implement robust authentication and authorization policies, monitor
user activity, detect suspicious behaviors, and mitigate the risk of malicious attacks.
Microsoft Entra is Microsoft's cloud-based identity provider. Other examples include Okta,
Ping identity, and many more.

Identity and access management (IAM) is the backbone of modern organizational security,
ensuring that the right individuals have idx_380f3cfe access to the right resources at the right times and for
the right reasons. At its core, IAM empowers businesses to manage digital identities and
control access to critical systems and data efficiently. By implementing IAM, organizations can
streamline authentication processes, reduce risks of unauthorized access, and ensure
regulatory compliance.
IAM systems provide the following functionality:
Identity management: This is the process of creating, storing, and managing identity
information.
Identity federation: Using identity federation, organizations can allow users to use
credentials from another system (for example, social identities like Google, Facebook,
or Apple) to gain access to their applications.
Provisioning and deprovisioning: This process involves creating user accounts,
controlling resource access, and assigning permissions.
Authentication: IAM systems idx_525733ef authenticate users, applications, and device identities by
confirming that they are who they claim to be. MFA and SSO can be applied at this
level.
Authorization: This idx_0d6dac65 ensures that users are granted the right access to the resources
that they need to access.
Access control: This process involves establishing user roles and permissions, as well
as implementing robust authentication and authorization protocols. Access controls
are employed to manage and restrict data access appropriately.
Reporting and monitoring: IAM systems can generate reports on sign-in times,
system accessed, types of authentication methods used to ensure compliance, and
highlight security risks.

Chapter 1 6
Figure 1.1: Authentication and authorization process
The user initiates an authentication request from the client application with the IdP. If the
credentials are valid, the IdP sends an ID token to the client application. The ID token contains
information about the user. The IdP idx_87c02ab2 obtains end-user consent and authorizes the client
application to access protected resources. Authorization is issued in the form of an access
token, which is subsequently transmitted to the client application. The access token is then
included with all future requests to the protected resource initiated by the client application.
Upon receiving a request, the resource server validates the access token; if validation succeeds,
the requested resources are made available, and a response is returned to the client
application.
Authentication and authorization standards
Before moving forward, it is important to idx_5ceede82 understand some of the commonly used
authentication and authorization standards.
OAuth
OAuth (Open Authorization) is a standard that allows users to authorize one app or service to
sign on to another without idx_b8a7c7ce revealing the password. It uses access tokens to prove a user's
identity and allows it to interact with another service on the user's behalf. A typical example is
websites showing messages like " Login with Facebook ". OAuth was originally designed for
websites and is not widely used today.
7 Introduction to Microsoft Entra
OAuth 2.0 is the latest release of idx_8a896f25 OAuth and is designed for both apps and websites. It
completely replaced OAuth and is now the industry standard for online authorization. It
provides consented access and restricts the actions that a client app can perform on a user's
behalf without sharing the user's credentials.
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)
SAML is an XML-based open idx_04ff5458 standard for securely exchanging authentication and
authorization data between an IdP and an application. It facilitates SSO, enabling users to
access multiple applications with a single idx_4441bb5c set of credentials. SAML ensures secure
communication through assertions, which carry information about user identity,
authentication, and permissions.
OpenID Connect (OIDC)
OIDC is an identity layer built on top idx_5ce13c18 of the OAuth 2.0 protocol, designed to idx_36e6283c simplify
authentication processes. It uses ID tokens to allow client applications to verify a user's
identity and obtain identity claims. It provides authentication while OAuth 2.0 provides
authorization. After the release of OpenID Connect that uses public-key encryption, OpenID
became a popular choice for the authentication layer for OAuth 2.0. It enables client
applications to authenticate users and retrieve their identity information idx_4e9f005c without requiring

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 6
chunks.content:
direct access to sensitive credentials. Like SAML, OIDC is used idx_7847baa4 for SSO but instead of XML, it
uses Representational State Transfer (REST) and JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). It is
designed to work with both native and mobile idx_78c402fc applications. It idx_692e3fe5 uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)
for securely sharing idx_7e1ce5cd identity assertions, allowing seamless integration across web apps, APIs,
and mobile platforms.
JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)
JWTs are open standard, compact, and URL-safe tokens used for securely transmitting
information between parties. JWTs are idx_78c1d1aa digitally signed and can be encrypted and
authenticated making them verifiable and trustworthy. They pass the identity of authenticated
users between the IdP and the service. They consist of three parts: a header, payload, and
signature. The header specifies the token type and signing algorithm, while the payload
contains claims about the user or application. The signature ensures the integrity and
authenticity of the token.
System for Cross-Domain Identity Management (SCIM)
SCIM is an open standard that idx_e3b2910e simplifies identity management by automating user
provisioning and deprovisioning across systems. It is particularly useful for ensuring
consistency in large-scale idx_d17410f2 environments where multiple applications require user data
synchronization. SCIM uses RESTful APIs and JSON, making it efficient for exchanging
information like user profiles and group memberships.

Web Services Federation (WS-Fed)
WS-Fed is a Microsoft-developed protocol idx_832be180 widely used in its applications to transport security
tokens for identity and authorization exchange. It facilitates the sharing of authentication and
authorization idx_e145d0b4 data between trusted domains, allowing users to access multiple applications
without repeatedly signing in. WS-Fed employs XML-based messaging to ensure
interoperability across platforms, supporting enterprise-level integration for web services. By
enabling SSO and identity delegation, WS-Fed enhances security and user convenience.
Microsoft Identity platform
The Microsoft identity platform is a comprehensive cloud-based identity service enabling
developers to create applications that idx_ae14ca8b support user authentication through Microsoft
identities or various social accounts. It facilitates secure access to an organization's proprietary
APIs as well as Microsoft APIs, such as Microsoft Graph. Using this, developers can build
idx_5eb3ab4e single-tenant line-of-business applications or multitenant Software-as-a-Service (SaaS)
applications.
There are several components that make idx_6ca1beb9 up the Microsoft identity platform. They are
described as follows:
Authentication service: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect standard-compliant
authentication service enables developers to authenticate various identity types like
Microsoft Entra ID accounts, personal Microsoft accounts, and social or local accounts
using Microsoft Entra External ID.
Open-source libraries: The Microsoft identity platform supports the Microsoft
Authentication Library (MSAL) and other idx_e216abbd standards-compliant libraries. Microsoft
recommends using MSAL as they provide support for Conditional Access scenarios,
SSO, token caching, and more.
Microsoft identity platform endpoint: The Microsoft identity platform endpoint is
OIDC certified. It works with MSAL and implements human readable scopes in
accordance with industry standards.
Application management portal: This is the Microsoft Entra admin center that
provides the configuration experience and other application management capabilities.
Application configuration API and PowerShell: The Microsoft identity platform
offers programmatic configuration capabilities of application using Microsoft Graph
API and PowerShell enabling organizations to automate DevOps tasks.
Developer content: This includes technical documentation, tutorials, API reference,
and code samples.

The following products are part of the Microsoft Entra family.
Microsoft Entra ID
Microsoft Entra ID, formerly idx_f93c0872 known as Azure Active Directory, is Microsoft's cloud-based
identity and access management solution. It idx_1ca30d14 provides basic identity, authentication,
authorization, and auditing for employees, business guests, devices, and applications. Using

IT administrators can use Entra ID to create and manage user accounts including employees

provide SSO capabilities to users. With these powerful tools, administrators can protect user

Microsoft Entra ID Governance
Microsoft Entra ID Governance is an identity governance solution that helps organizations
improve productivity, strengthen security, and meet regulatory requirements. Using this,
administrators can ensure that the idx_3c5a6079 right users have access to the right resources. It helps
organizations mitigate identity and access risks by protecting, monitoring, and auditing access
to resources.
Microsoft Entra ID Governance helps organizations remain compliant by:
Ensuring that the right users have access to the right resources
Understanding how the users are using that access
Ensure that there are controls in place to manage access
Facilitate auditing to ensure that the controls are working effectively
Using Microsoft Entra ID Governance, organizations can govern the identity and access
lifecycle of employees and business guests and ensure secure privileged access for
administrators.
Transactions per hour and object count are guidelines and not product limitations.
These are provided to enable selection of the appropriate plan.

13 Introduction to Microsoft Entra
Identity and access lifecycle
Each identity goes through a lifecycle idx_67c1aaf0 from the time an employee joins the organization to the
time they leave. During this time, they may hold different positions and move across the
organization. This is known as the joiner-mover-leaver scenario as shown in the idx_939d80d8 following
figure:
Figure 1.4: Identity and access lifecycle
In most organizations when a user joins, their identity is created in the Human Capital
Management (HCM) system. Organizations idx_44fec3fc should be able to automate onboarding of users
from HCM to the identity system so that they can be productive on day 1. Microsoft Entra ID
Governance has the following idx_46b3926c capabilities that can help organizations automate the identity
and access management lifecycle:
Inbound provisioning from HCM systems: Microsoft Entra offers out-of-the-box
capabilities to retrieve identities from Workday and SuccessFactors and automatically
create those identities in Microsoft Entra ID and Active Directory.
Lifecycle workflows: They are used to automate mundane tasks at different stages in
the identity lifecycle. These workflows can be triggered based on certain events like

Privileged access lifecycle
Organizations also need to govern privileged accounts to prevent misuse and ensure that
administrators have the right permissions to perform the idx_094f4842 tasks that they need to complete.
Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) helps provide just-in-time access to
administrators. Just-in-time access is idx_55deecd1 an approach that ensures administrators receive the
precise permissions they need for a specific task for a limited duration. This minimizes risks by
reducing the exposure of sensitive systems to over-permissioned accounts. PIM helps
implement this model by enabling temporary access to high-level permissions. By requiring
approval workflows, monitoring, and expiration of elevated rights, organizations can prevent
misuse and enhance security.
Licensing
Microsoft Entra ID Governance idx_fc82b2bf offers advanced identity governance capabilities to Microsoft
Entra ID P1 and P2 customers. They are available as two products – Microsoft Entra ID
Governance and Microsoft Entra ID Governance Step up for Microsoft Entra ID P2.
These two products have the basic identity governance features that are part of Microsoft Entra
ID P2. Additionally, they have more advanced identity governance features. The identity
governance features are the same in both products. The only difference is that they have
different prerequisites.
To purchase an Entra ID Governance license, the tenant needs an active subscription to AAD
Premium or AAD Premium P2. This requirement is met if you have Microsoft Entra ID P1,
Microsoft 365 E3/E5, EMS E3/E5, or Microsoft 365 F1/F3.
To purchase Microsoft Entra ID Governance step up for Microsoft Entra ID P2, the tenant needs
AAD Premium P2. This requirement is met if you have Microsoft Entra ID P2, Microsoft 365 E5,
EMS E5, M365 E5/F5 Security, or M365 F5 Security + Compliance.
Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management will be covered in detail in Chapter 8,

Microsoft Entra Identity Protection
Microsoft Entra Identity Protection helps idx_7974b429 organizations detect, investigate, and respond to
identity-based risks. These risks can be used to enforce risk-based Conditional Access policies
or idx_a7059704 be sent to a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) tool for investigation.
Microsoft receives trillions of risk signals every day from sources like Microsoft Accounts,
Microsoft 365, Xbox, and more. These signals help detect risky behavior like atypical travel,
anonymous IP addresses, password spray attacks, leaked credentials, and more. Each time a
user attempts to sign in, ID protection checks in real time if the user or the sign-in attempt is

Microsoft Entra Verified ID
Decentralized Identities (DIDs) represent a transformative approach to identity
management. Unlike traditional systems that rely idx_706011f4 on centralized entities, DIDs allow
individuals to manage their own identity information securely. By leveraging blockchain or
distributed ledger technologies, DIDs ensure that users retain control over their personal data,
reducing reliance on third-party providers. This innovation empowers users with greater
privacy and autonomy, fostering trust in digital interactions.
Based on open DID standards, Microsoft Entra Verified ID enables organizations to issue
verifiable credentials to users that can be stored on their personal devices. They can then
present these digital credentials to any organization when they want to prove their identity.
For example, Sally works for Contoso. Contoso has issued Verified ID to their employees which
Sally has stored in a wallet on her phone. When she applies for a home loan, the bank offers
discounted interest rates to Contoso employees. Sally uses the Verified ID stored on her phone
to prove that she is an employee of Contoso. The wallet application records the transaction to
show where Sally used her proof of employment.

Microsoft Entra Workload ID
Each entity that requires authentication has an identity. At a high level, there are two types of
identities: human and idx_744e4043 machine/non-human. Human identities are assigned to individual
users, while machine or non-human identities are used by devices, applications, and services.
The following image shows this in detail:
Figure 1.5: Machine and human identities
In Microsoft Entra, identities used by applications, service principals, and managed identities
are called workload identities. Microsoft idx_39222a76 Entra Workload ID is the identity and access
management solution for workload identities.
